title: Toll Slide
statement: A delivery cart crosses a toll grid from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell. grid[r][c] is the toll for being in cell (r, c): the cart pays the toll of its starting cell and of every cell it moves into. A normal move goes one cell right or one cell down. Once per trip, instead of a normal move, the cart may take the service slide: it glides any number of cells (at least one) to the right along its current row, paying nothing for any cell it passes or lands on. Return the smallest total toll for the trip. The slide is optional.
constraints: 1 <= grid[r].length <= 150, and every row has the same length

examples.explanation: Pay 4 for the start, slide along the top row to the last column for free, then move down onto 1 and 7. The total is 4 + 1 + 7 = 12. Without the slide, the cheapest right/down trip costs 27 (4 + 7 + 2 + 6 + 1 + 7).
The cart starts on the goal and pays the toll of that one cell.

hints.content: Ignoring the slide, this is the familiar right-and-down grid walk. What extra fact must a partly finished trip remember because of the slide?
Whether the slide has already been used changes what the cart can do next, so keep two costs per cell: arriving with the slide still unused and arriving with it already used.

The unused layer is the usual cheaper of the cell above and the cell to the left, plus the toll. The used layer comes from above or from the left in the used layer plus the toll, or from a slide that started somewhere earlier in the same row.

A slide ending in cell (r, c) can start from any earlier cell of row r in the unused layer and costs nothing extra. Keep the cheapest unused arrival seen so far in the row as you sweep it left to right.

The answer is the smaller of the two layers at the bottom-right cell. This runs in O(rows * cols) with two rolling rows. Trying every slide start for every cell is O(rows * cols^2), and trying every trip is exponential.

testCases.explanation: Sliding across the top row is much cheaper than any ordinary trip.
A single row: pay for the start and slide the rest of the way for free.
A single column: the slide cannot help, so all four tolls are paid.
The cheapest trip steps down to the second row first and slides along it; sliding along the top row would cost more because the last column is expensive in the second row.
A random 14 by 14 grid, already too large for trying every trip.
A random grid at the largest size, 150 rows by 133 columns.
A 100 by 150 grid with a diagonal band of cheap cells among expensive ones.

solutions.title: Try every trip, with and without a slide
solutions.intuition: Follow every possible sequence of moves, including every possible slide length, and keep the cheapest total.
solutions.approach: Recurse from the top-left with the toll paid so far and a flag for whether the slide was used. Branch on moving down, moving right, and (when unused) sliding to every later column of the row. At the goal, record the minimum.
solutions.pseudocode:
walk(r, c, paid, used): if at goal: best = min(best, paid)
  down: walk(r+1, c, paid + grid[r+1][c], used)
  right: walk(r, c+1, paid + grid[r][c+1], used)
  if not used: for target > c: walk(r, target, paid, true)
solutions.timeComplexity: Exponential in rows + cols (every monotone path times every slide)
commonMistakes: Charging for cells the slide passes over.
Allowing a second slide, or a slide of length zero.
Forgetting that the starting cell is paid.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Enumerating every trip is correct and shows the structure, but the number of trips is a binomial coefficient times the slide choices, so it collapses beyond a 10 by 10 grid. The same cell and slide flag are reached by many trips, which dynamic programming exploits.

steps.title: Walk the slide trip
steps.content: In the first example the trip pays 4, slides along row 0 to column 3 for nothing, then pays 1 and 7.

steps.title: Compare
steps.content: Every other trip costs at least 12 as well, so the minimum is 12.

solutions.title: Two layers, scanning every possible slide start
solutions.intuition: Only the cell and whether the slide is used matter, not how the cart got there, so keep a table for each case.
solutions.approach: plain[r][c] is the cheapest arrival with the slide unused and slid[r][c] with it used. Plain comes from above or left. Slid comes from above or left in slid, or from plain[r][from] for every earlier column in the same row (the free slide). The answer is the smaller at the corner.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(rows * cols^2): at most 150 * 150 * 150 = 3.4 million steps
commonMistakes: Adding the toll of the landing cell after a slide.
Letting slid start from slid at the same cell, so a second slide sneaks in.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This is the direct dynamic program: two states per cell, with the slide transition checked against every earlier column. The extra factor of the row width comes from re-scanning the row for each cell, which the running minimum removes.

steps.title: Fill the plain layer
steps.content: plain is the ordinary cheapest trip cost to each cell, e.g. 4 at the start and 11 at (0, 1).

steps.title: Fill the slid layer
steps.content: slid at (0, 3) is plain[0][0] = 4 because the slide from the start is free, and slid at (2, 3) is 4 + 1 + 7 = 12.

solutions.title: Two layers with a running minimum along the row
solutions.intuition: The best place to start a slide that lands in column c is the cheapest unused arrival anywhere to its left in the same row, and that minimum can be carried along as the row is swept.
solutions.approach: Sweep each row left to right with rolling arrays for plain and slid. At each column compute plain from above/left, compute slid as the smaller of (slid from above/left + toll) and the cheapest plain value seen earlier in this row, then update that running minimum with the new plain value.
solutions.pseudocode:
for r: cheapestLeft = inf
  for c: plain[c] = min(plain above, plain left) + toll
         slid[c] = min(min(slid above, slid left) + toll, cheapestLeft)
         cheapestLeft = min(cheapestLeft, plain[c])
return min(plain[last], slid[last])
commonMistakes: Updating cheapestLeft before computing slid, which lets a slide have length zero.
Resetting cheapestLeft only once instead of at the start of each row.
Forgetting to carry both layers between rows.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Two states per cell turn an exponential search into 2 * rows * cols values. The only non-local transition is the slide, and since it always starts from an earlier cell of the same row, a running minimum answers it in O(1). Rolling the rows keeps memory at one row.

steps.title: Row 0
steps.content: plain along row 0 is 4, 11, 13, 22; the running minimum before column 3 is 4, so slid at column 3 is 4.

steps.title: Row 2
steps.content: Moving down from slid at (1, 3) = 5 gives 5 + 7 = 12 at (2, 3), which beats plain there (27), so the answer is 12.
